slides.title: Reports change for two different reasons
keyPoints: Meaning: count or warning classification.
Presentation: plain text or brackets.
Negative counts remain invalid in either format.
slides.narration: Our inspection tool must present the same count on two screens. One wants count equals six; another wants count colon six inside brackets. The tool also needs a warning report that chooses high above five and normal otherwise. We now have two reasons for change: what the report means and how the text looks. Begin by stating those reasons separately. A punctuation change should not force us to rethink the warning boundary, and a policy change should not force us to edit every format. The program builds strings in memory; its Writer name does not mean that it writes a file or contacts a service.
actions: Create a two-by-two table of report meaning and output format.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Two useful reports, two useful formats

question.prompt: What two choices form the four report combinations?
question.answer: Count versus warning report, and plain versus bracket formatting.

slides.title: One report needs only one function
keyPoints: Validate the count.
Build one clear result string.
Do not split a dimension that does not vary yet.
slides.narration: This first program serves exactly one requirement: render a valid count in the plain format. A single function makes the contract visible and keeps the implementation short. The function returns a string value, so the caller owns the returned characters. It throws before formatting a negative number because negativity is a report-domain error. There is no need yet for an abstract Writer or a family of Report classes. We will earn that separation by showing independent changes, rather than adding it in anticipation of every possible future request. Notice that a valid zero is accepted; absence of work is still a meaningful count.
actions: Run with six and zero.
Explain why the negative test belongs before formatting.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch07.json → Two useful reports, two useful formats

question.prompt: Would a Writer interface improve a permanently fixed single report?
question.answer: Not necessarily. The direct function is easier to read when there is no independent format choice.

slides.title: A policy edit can drift between formats
keyPoints: New requirement: high only above ten.
Plain output was updated.
Bracket output still applies the old boundary.
slides.narration: Imagine that an operations team changes the warning boundary from five to ten. In a combined implementation, each format has its own copy of the classification expression. A developer fixes the plain version but misses the bracket version. The two strings now disagree about the same observation even though both compile and run normally. Our demonstration uses the new requirement deliberately; the chapter's unchanged main example still uses five. This is the pressure that motivates a bridge. Put the classification decision in one report path, and let separate writers control punctuation. We need a boundary that prevents this kind of drift from spreading across combinations.
actions: Predict whether the two outputs agree before running.
Locate the duplicated business decision, not just duplicated punctuation.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch07.json → Locate the two decisions before drawing classes

question.prompt: Which concern was duplicated and then changed inconsistently?
question.answer: The warning classification threshold was duplicated in each formatting function.

slides.title: Separate meaning from punctuation
keyPoints: Report chooses a field name and validates data.
Writer formats the supplied field without changing meaning.
The stored Writer connection selects the pairing.
slides.narration: We can now name the design. Bridge keeps two related families connected through a stable operation so that they can grow independently. In this chapter, CountReport and WarningReport decide the meaning of the field. Plain and Brackets decide how that field is written. Report stores a borrowed Writer connection, and each concrete report crosses that connection during render. With two reports and two writers, we have four supported pairings but do not need four combination classes. This is not a promise that every imaginable display can use the same tiny operation. Independence only holds while the shared field contract carries the data each supported format needs.
actions: Point to the single classification expression in WarningReport.
Point to punctuation in each Writer implementation.

question.prompt: Which side should change when brackets become braces?
question.answer: The formatting implementation should change; the report classification should remain the same.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Support count and warning reports in both formats.
Classify n > 5 as high; zero through five as normal.
Reject negative counts before formatting.
slides.narration:
Counts in plain text and brackets. Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit.

Support count and warning reports in both formats. Classify n > 5 as high; zero through five as normal. Reject negative counts before formatting.

Reports never change a writer or own its lifetime. Writers preserve the supplied name and numeric value. Validation happens before formatting. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. An enum-based formatter is simpler for a permanently closed set of formats. Templates fit compile-time selection; virtual writers fit objects selected while the program runs.

comparisons.text: Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit.

comparisons.label: A reasonable alternative
comparisons.text: An enum-based formatter is simpler for a permanently closed set of formats. Templates fit compile-time selection; virtual writers fit objects selected while the program runs.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Bridge implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Reports never change a writer or own its lifetime. Writers preserve the supplied name and numeric value. Validation happens before formatting.

slides.title: Two useful reports, two useful formats
keyPoints: A small inspection tool prints a count and also classifies that count.
The simplest first version returns a string directly from a function.
slides.narration:
A small inspection tool prints a count and also classifies that count. One screen wants count=6. Another wants [count:6]. The classification report calls counts above five high and all others normal. It must work in either format. Negative counts are invalid. Requirements now vary in two directions: what the report means, and how its fields are written.

The simplest first version returns a string directly from a function. That is a good solution when there is one meaning and one format. A second function can serve a second fixed report. The difficulty appears when both dimensions grow. If each combination has its own class, two report types and two formats need four combinations. Three types and four formats need twelve. The count is the product of the choices, not automatically an exponential function of one choice. What hurts is repeated policy and repeated formatting.

question.prompt: How many combinations arise from two report meanings and two output formats? What changes when a third format is added?
question.answer: There are four combinations, then six. Writing a subclass for every combination duplicates policy and formatting. The next step separates the two choices so they can be combined.

slides.title: Locate the two decisions before drawing classes
keyPoints: Suppose the warning boundary changes from five to ten.
A bridge is a stable connection between a high-level operation and a lower-level implementation that can vary independently.
The pattern's traditional word abstraction means the high-level view offered to the caller.
slides.narration:
Suppose the warning boundary changes from five to ten. In the combined design, each warning-format class must change. Suppose the bracket screen changes its separator. Every bracket-report class must change. That gives a concrete reason to separate the decisions. The boundary rule belongs with the report; punctuation belongs with the writer. Neither side should inspect the exact type on the other side.

A bridge is a stable connection between a high-level operation and a lower-level implementation that can vary independently. Here Report supplies the high-level render operation and borrows a Writer. CountReport and WarningReport decide which field name to send. Plain and Brackets implement Writer::field. The bridge is the writer_ reference. The two families can now grow without adding one class for every cross-product combination.

The pattern's traditional word abstraction means the high-level view offered to the caller. It does not require every high-level class to be an abstract C++ base class. Our Report is abstract because two report meanings already exist and both must be usable through the same contract. A single concrete report with a Writer member would still separate format from meaning when only one report is needed.

slides.title: Trace data and control across the bridge
keyPoints: In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them.
WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first.
The returned strings own their character storage.
slides.narration:
In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them. cp stores a reference to plain; cb stores a reference to brackets. Calling cb.render(6) enters CountReport. validate first rejects a negative value. The report then sends the label count and integer 6 to writer_.field. Virtual dispatch selects Brackets::field. It creates [count:6] and returns that string by value through the report to main.

WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first. The conditional expression n > 5 ? "high" : "normal" evaluates the condition, selects exactly one of the two strings, and initializes label. The question mark introduces the true result, and the colon separates it from the false result. This colon is different from the colon that begins a constructor initializer list or a range loop. Syntax takes its meaning from its surrounding statement.

The returned strings own their character storage. The label passed to field is a const reference, so field borrows the argument during the call. Neither writer keeps that reference afterward. writer_ is a longer-lived borrow stored inside Report. Those are different lifetime obligations: a call parameter need only stay valid for the call, while a stored reference must stay valid for later calls too.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → What compilation guarantees and what it cannot
slides.title: What compilation guarantees and what it cannot
keyPoints: The compiler checks public inheritance, virtual signatures, and whether each concrete class implements the required operation.
The compiler does not verify that a new Writer preserves the label and value faithfully.
At execution the same report can use either writer selected during construction.
slides.narration:
The compiler checks public inheritance, virtual signatures, and whether each concrete class implements the required operation. override catches a mismatch. protected makes writer_ and validate available to the derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. The helper is static because it depends only on its argument and needs no Report object. Constructors initialize the reference before any render call can occur.

The compiler does not verify that a new Writer preserves the label and value faithfully. A writer could accidentally swap field names or drop a minus sign. That would still compile. The shared semantic contract is therefore essential: format the supplied name and integer without changing their meaning. The report checks the domain rule that counts cannot be negative. The generic writer is capable of formatting any integer, which makes it usable in other domains.

At execution the same report can use either writer selected during construction. Our design does not provide a setter to switch writer_ later; C++ references cannot be rebound. To change format, construct a new report borrowing another writer. This keeps ownership and configuration simple. An application needing live format changes could instead hold a non-owning pointer with an explicit non-null rule or own an interchangeable writer. That requirement has not appeared here, so its extra states are unnecessary.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → When the split helps, and when it does not
slides.title: When the split helps, and when it does not
keyPoints: A bridge gives independence only when the interface is stable and truthful.
An enum and one formatting function may be smaller when the set of formats is fixed and tiny.
Bridge and Adapter can produce similar shapes in a diagram.
slides.narration:
A bridge gives independence only when the interface is stable and truthful. If field lacks data one format needs, reports may begin checking for special writers. That is a warning that the boundary is too narrow or the supposedly independent dimensions are actually linked. Improve the contract using a real use case, or accept a smaller set of supported combinations. Do not promise that every conceivable report will work with every renderer.

An enum and one formatting function may be smaller when the set of formats is fixed and tiny. A template can select a writer at compilation and may remove virtual calls, but it exposes more implementation to callers and moves the choice from runtime to build time. Neither alternative is inherently inferior. The reason for this bridge is the already demonstrated independent growth in report policy and presentation.

Bridge and Adapter can produce similar shapes in a diagram. Their motivations differ. An adapter repairs an existing disagreement between interfaces. A bridge deliberately separates dimensions that should evolve independently. When reviewing a change, ask what boundary is being protected. Add tests for each report's meaning and each format's text, plus a few combinations. That protects the separation more effectively than checking only class names.

question.prompt: Does sharing a const Writer reference guarantee thread safety?
question.answer: No general guarantee follows from const alone. A concrete writer could use mutable state or external resources; its implementation must supply any concurrency guarantee.

slides.title: The abstraction role is not C++ syntax
keyPoints: Report is the high-level view offered to clients.
Writer is the lower-level formatting contract.
A Bridge can also use a concrete high-level class.
slides.narration: The traditional pattern word abstraction means the useful high-level view, not automatically an abstract C++ class. Here Report happens to be abstract because several report meanings need the same render operation. A single concrete report holding a Writer could still separate meaning from formatting. This distinction matters in reviews: counting abstract classes is not evidence that a bridge exists. Look instead for independently changing decisions connected through a useful operation. Writer::field receives a name and a number because these are the stable pieces of information both current formats can display. It should not ask which concrete report made the request.
actions: Ask whether one concrete CountReport plus two writers could still preserve the separation.

question.prompt: Is an abstract C++ Report base required for every Bridge?
question.answer: No. The separation of independently varying responsibilities is central; an abstract high-level base depends on the actual caller needs.

theory.what: High-level reporting delegates formatting through a stable contract.
theory.where: Report holds writer_; concrete render methods call field.
theory.why: Meaning and appearance should change independently.
theory.invariant: Each writer preserves the supplied field meaning.
theory.risk: Type checks against concrete reports or writers recouple the families.

slides.title: Trace one value across the connection
keyPoints: CountReport validates six.
Writer receives the name count and value six.
Brackets returns [count:6] by value.
slides.narration: Follow cb.render with six. The selected object is a CountReport whose stored reference points to the Brackets object. CountReport first checks the domain rule, then calls writer_.field with count and six. The compiler checks that Writer offers this operation. Runtime virtual dispatch chooses the Brackets implementation. That implementation creates a new string and returns it through the report to the client. Data moves across the bridge as a field name and integer; control moves into the chosen writer and then back. No writer reference to the temporary name is saved. That makes the short call-time borrow safe under the current contract.
actions: Trace forward with arrows for calls, then backward with the returned string.

question.prompt: Where is the punctuation decision made for cb.render(6)?
question.answer: Inside Brackets::field, after CountReport validates the count and supplies the field name.

theory.what: A report call delegates formatting once and returns the resulting value.
theory.why: The report should not know bracket punctuation.
theory.invariant: The passed integer and name retain their meaning.
theory.risk: A writer that retains a reference to a temporary argument can later access dead storage.

slides.title: Two references, two lifetime duties
keyPoints: field borrows its name only during the call.
Report borrows its writer across many calls.
A reference member cannot be rebound.
slides.narration: The same ampersand can appear in two places with different practical obligations. The field parameter borrows a string only while that one function call is active. The writer_ member is stored in Report and may be used much later. Its source writer must therefore outlive all those report calls. In main, writers are constructed first, followed by reports, which gives the correct reverse destruction order. The reference also fixes the pairing during construction: assigning through a reference does not make it refer to another object. A runtime format switch would need a new report or a deliberately different connection design, with its own rules.
actions: Draw the short argument lifetime inside the longer report and writer lifetimes.

question.prompt: Can a setter rebind the existing const Writer& member?
question.answer: No. Construct a new report or redesign the connection as an explicitly managed pointer or owner if live switching is required.

theory.what: A report stores a non-owning connection selected at construction.
theory.why: Writers can be shared without copying their objects.
theory.invariant: The selected writer stays alive for each render call.
theory.risk: Returning a report that borrows a local writer creates a dangling connection.

slides.title: Syntax does not enforce semantic honesty
keyPoints: override catches a wrong virtual signature.
protected limits member access to the class family.
Tests still verify labels, thresholds, and formatting.
slides.narration: The compiler provides several useful checks, but none can read the business requirement. Protected makes writer_ and validate available to derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. Static on validate means it uses no particular Report object's data. The conditional expression in WarningReport evaluates n greater than five and selects high or normal; its colon separates the two possible results. Override catches a mismatched field or render signature. However, a writer that changes six to seven still satisfies the type signature. Tests must verify that formatting preserves data and that the report chooses the correct label on both sides of the threshold.

Ask which guarantees are checked by compilation and which need examples or tests.

question.prompt: Why test five and six rather than only a large count?
question.answer: They exercise the exact branch boundary: five is normal and six is high in the chapter contract.

theory.what: Language checks establish valid calls; tests establish required meaning.
theory.why: Independent components must share more than a matching signature.
theory.invariant: Every supported writer preserves the report-selected field and count.
theory.risk: Silent semantic changes compile successfully and can disagree across formats.

slides.title: Add CSV by extending one side
slides.eyebrow: MAINTENANCE / A TEST OF THE BOUNDARY
keyPoints: Add Csv::field without rewriting reports.
Test count, high, normal, and zero.
Fixed safe labels do not make a general CSV library.
slides.narration: The extension asks for comma-separated output. The useful test of our design is whether this format can be added without changing either report's decision logic. Csv implements field and joins the supplied name, a comma, and the number. That is sufficient for the existing fixed labels, because count, high, and normal contain no comma or quote. Do not claim that the result is a complete CSV encoder for arbitrary text. If labels become user-controlled, quoting and escaping become new requirements. A clear boundary makes that change local, but a boundary cannot eliminate the need to define the new format contract.
actions: Review the solution and verify that CountReport and WarningReport are unchanged.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → When the split helps, and when it does not

question.prompt: Why is name + comma + value sufficient only for this lab contract?
question.answer: The supported fixed names contain no CSV-special characters. Arbitrary names would need escaping and quoting rules.

keyPoints: A report borrows one formatting mechanism and protects the count rule.
All formats receive validated report inputs without duplicating the validation.

slides.narration:
A report borrows one formatting mechanism and protects the count rule. These protected members support both concrete report types. All formats receive validated report inputs without duplicating the validation.

question.prompt: Explain Bridge without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit. An enum-based formatter is simpler for a permanently closed set of formats. Templates fit compile-time selection; virtual writers fit objects selected while the program runs.

slides.title: Independence has a price and a limit
keyPoints: Two types and four formats create eight combinations.
Separation reduces repeated implementation decisions.
A weak shared contract can force coupling back in.
slides.narration: Bridge is useful because the number of combinations grows as the product of the two choices. Two reports and four formats create eight possible pairings. Separate families can avoid writing a dedicated class for every pairing, but the combination behavior still needs thought and testing. If a new format requires information that field does not carry, forcing it into the interface may create special cases or concrete-type checks. That is evidence to revisit the contract. Sometimes an enum and a small switch is clearer for a closed set. The design is successful when real changes remain local, not when the diagram contains more boxes.

slides.title: Bridge and Adapter can look alike
keyPoints: Bridge separates dimensions expected to vary.
Adapter repairs an existing interface mismatch.
A stored service connection alone proves neither pattern.
slides.narration: Both designs can show one object forwarding a call to another. That shared shape does not settle their purpose. In Adapter, a useful old service and an established caller disagree about an interface or meaning. In Bridge, we intentionally put reporting and formatting behind a connection so each side can develop independently. A real system can even place an adapter on one side of a bridge. The useful review question is therefore what change this boundary protects against. Here, adding a writer should not duplicate report policy. That story identifies Bridge more clearly than simply noticing a reference member.

question.prompt: Can similar UML class shapes represent different patterns?
question.answer: Yes. Pattern intent, responsibilities, and the protected change boundary distinguish them.

slides.title: Defend a new report in plain language
keyPoints: Name the policy change.
State what Writer must receive.
Predict which existing tests remain unchanged.
slides.narration: Imagine adding a report that labels values above twenty as critical and others as routine. Before writing code, explain why the new labels belong to the report and why every current writer can still display them. Then ask whether the CSV contract remains safe with these fixed words. Existing CountReport and WarningReport tests should stay untouched because their rules have not changed. Add focused tests around twenty and twenty-one and test the new report with more than one writer. This exercise turns a memorized pattern into a maintenance plan: identify the changing responsibility, preserve the shared promise, and verify both the new decision and old behavior.
